How parametricboot is validated

Source: vignettes/validation.Rmd
validation.Rmd

Scope of the claims

The parametric bootstrap samples from an assumed, fitted model. Reproducing that model’s known distribution, refitting it correctly, and computing summaries correctly are distinct validation obligations. Passing these checks does not establish model adequacy for a new dataset, nor does it give universal finite-sample coverage guarantees.

Four kinds of evidence are useful:

  1. Simulation identity: compare simulated outcomes or refitted statistics against calculations made independently of the package implementation.
  2. Analytical benchmark: compare a procedure with a known exact result under stated conditions.
  3. Reproducibility: fixed seeds and consistent serial/parallel results ensure that a change does not silently alter the experiment.
  4. Coverage experiments: repeat the entire data-generating experiment and measure the frequency with which intervals contain the true parameter. This is a separate outer simulation, not one fitted-model bootstrap run.

The tests in tests/testthat/ contain numerical checks. This vignette illustrates the reasoning, with deliberately small, reproducible examples.

Gaussian linear model: theoretical coefficient uncertainty

For y = X beta + epsilon, with independent Gaussian residuals of variance sigma^2 and full-column-rank fixed X, the sampling covariance of ordinary least-squares coefficients is sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1} when sigma is the true residual scale.

library(parametricboot)
data(mtcars)
model <- stats::lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
boot <- pb_simulate(model, n = 300, seed = 102)
coefs <- boot$estimates[!boot$failed, , drop = FALSE]
empirical_sd <- apply(coefs, 2L, stats::sd)
reference_sd <- sqrt(diag(stats::vcov(model)))
data.frame(
  term = names(empirical_sd),
  bootstrap_sd = unname(empirical_sd),
  plug_in_reference_sd = unname(reference_sd)
)
#>          term bootstrap_sd plug_in_reference_sd
#> 1 (Intercept)  1.625133217           1.59878754
#> 2          wt  0.632272912           0.63273349
#> 3          hp  0.008840726           0.00902971

The analytical calculation uses the fitted variance as a plug-in approximation to the unknown generating variance. At finite bootstrap replicate counts, empirical and analytical standard errors are not expected to match exactly. They should be evaluated with Monte Carlo uncertainty in mind. A normal regression coefficient has an exact Student t confidence interval under the classical regression assumptions; this is a useful benchmark for studentisation, not a guarantee about arbitrary models.

Prediction uncertainty: a variance identity

For a new Gaussian observation, the law of total variance separates the spread of conditional means across bootstrap refits from the expected residual variance. The latter is nonzero even if every bootstrap refit has identical coefficients.

newdata <- mtcars[1:2, c("wt", "hp")]
variance <- pb_predict_variance(boot, newdata)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  variance$total_variance,
  variance$parameter_variance + variance$observation_variance
)))
variance
#>   prediction parameter_variance observation_variance total_variance
#> 1   23.57233          0.3006903             6.712599       7.013289
#> 2   22.58348          0.2771760             6.712599       6.989775
#>   successful_replicates
#> 1                   300
#> 2                   300

For Poisson regression the conditional observation variance is the fitted mean; for negative-binomial regression it is mu + mu^2/theta, with theta re-estimated by each refit. The test suite independently evaluates these identities. Prediction intervals additionally depend on quantiles and cannot be validated by a variance identity alone.

Goodness of fit: distinguish simulation precision from model validity

A bootstrap goodness-of-fit p-value compares the observed statistic against statistics simulated under the fitted null model. For B successful replicates and k simulated values at least as extreme as the observed, the add-one tail estimate is (k + 1)/(B + 1). This is not a statement that the null model has a particular posterior probability of being true.

The Monte Carlo uncertainty of the simulated tail count is distinct from uncertainty about the statistical model. pb_gof_mc_error() provides diagnostics for the former. The same distinction applies to confidence interval endpoints: more replicates reduce Monte Carlo error, but cannot repair systematic model misspecification.

What to verify before extending model support

A new model class requires an independently checked response simulator, correct handling of weights and offsets, preservation of model structure under refitting, and tests of dispersion or nuisance-parameter re-estimation. Unsupported class/family combinations are intentionally rejected rather than treated as ordinary GLMs.

Further useful validation includes nested-model likelihood-ratio comparisons against exact F tests when applicable, mixed-model replicates compared with lme4::bootMer(), and survival-model baseline-hazard checks against survival::survfit(). Existing dedicated regression tests are the appropriate source for those model-specific numerical identities.

Limits and references

No finite list of tests can prove a statistical procedure reliable under arbitrary data-generating mechanisms. Conditional simulation checks, independent mathematical benchmarks, model criticism, and repeated-sampling coverage studies answer different questions and should be reported separately.

  • Davison, A. C. and Hinkley, D. V. (1997). Bootstrap Methods and Their Application. Cambridge University Press.
  • Efron, B. and Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall.
  • Hall, P. (1992). The Bootstrap and Edgeworth Expansion. Springer.
